<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
$R_{\mathbb{F}_2}(\langle 3,3,3\rangle)=23$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:integer}
A bilinear algorithm over $\mathbb{F}_2$ or with integer coefficients that multiplies two $3\times 3$ matrices uses at least $23$ multiplications. In particular $R_{\mathbb{Z}}(\langle 3,3,3\rangle)=23$, and no recursive $3\times3$ algorithm with integer constants has an exponent below $\log_3 23\approx 2.854$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:cap}
If $T=\sum_{s=1}^{r}a_s\otimes b_s\otimes c_s$, then for every subspace $S\subseteq A$
\[
\#\{s : a_s\in S\}\le r-R(S).
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Applying $\pi_S\otimes 1\otimes 1$ removes the terms with $a_s\in S$ and leaves a decomposition of $T_S$ of length $\#\{s:a_s\notin S\}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:point}
If $S$ is spanned by a matrix of rank one, then $R(S)\ge 21$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:distinct}
The $22$ first factors of a decomposition of length $22$ are pairwise distinct.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
A repeated first factor $a$ would put two first factors in the point $\mathbb{F}_2 a$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:point} and \cite{RR26} all points have $R\ge 21$ and therefore capacity at most $1$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:raise}
The lower bounds of Table~\ref{tab:raise} hold.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:split}
$\sum_t\operatorname{rank}(a_t)\ge 27$, that is, $\Delta\ge 0$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
$27=\operatorname{rank} P\le\sum_t\operatorname{rank} M(a_t,b_t,c_t)=\sum_t\operatorname{rank}(a_t)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:gram}
The matrix $\Gamma=Y^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}X$ is idempotent of rank $27$, and $\Pi=I+\Gamma$ is idempotent of rank $\Delta$. Its blocks are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gram}
\Gamma_{ts}=R_t^{\mathsf T}B_sC_tL_s .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$\Gamma^2=Y^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}(XY^{\mathsf T})P^{-1}X=\Gamma$. The rank of $\Gamma$ is at most $27$, and $X\Gamma Y^{\mathsf T}=P$ has rank $27$, so $\operatorname{rank}\Gamma=27$. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the matrix $I+\Gamma=I-\Gamma$ is the complementary idempotent, of rank $(27+\Delta)-27$. For \eqref{eq:gram}, $P^{-1}=P^{\mathsf T}$ and $P^{\mathsf T}_{(j,\gamma),(i,\beta)}=1$ exactly when $\beta=jk$ and $\gamma=ki$ for some $k$. Hence the $(\alpha,\alpha')$ entry of $\Gamma_{ts}$ is $\sum_{i,j,k}(R_t)_{j\alpha}(B_s)_{jk}(C_t)_{ki}(L_s)_{i\alpha'}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:S}
If $\Delta=0$ and some first factor is invertible, then $r=25$. In particular, a decomposition of length $22$ with $\Delta=0$ has type $(17,5,0)$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For $\Delta=0$, \eqref{eq:excess} reads $a_tB_sC_ta_s=\delta_{ts}a_t$. Let $a_0$ be invertible. Then $a_0B_0C_0a_0=a_0$ gives $B_0C_0=a_0^{-1}$, so $C_0$ is invertible. For $s\ne 0$ the equation $a_0B_sC_0a_s=0$ shows that $B_s$ vanishes on $C_0\,\mathrm{col}(a_s)$, a space of dimension $r_s$. Hence $\operatorname{rank} B_s\le 3-r_s$. The equation $a_sB_sC_sa_s=a_s$ gives $r_s\le\operatorname{rank} B_s$. Therefore $r_s\le 3-r_s$, that is $r_s=1$, for all $s\ne 0$. Then $27=\sum_tr_t=3+(r-1)$. For $r=22$ there is therefore no invertible first factor, and $n_1+n_2=22$, $n_1+2n_2=27$ give $(17,5,0)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:S3}
A decomposition with three distinct invertible first factors has $\Delta\ge 2$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:S} we may assume $\Delta=1$, so that $\Pi=pq^{\mathsf T}$ with $q^{\mathsf T}p=1$. Let $x,y$ range over the indices of the three invertible terms, take $L_x=a_x$ and $R_x=I$, and let $p_x,q_x\in\mathbb{F}_2^3$ be the blocks of $p$ and $q$. Since $\Gamma=I+\Pi$, \eqref{eq:gram} gives
\[
Z_{yx}:=B_yC_x=(\delta_{xy}I+p_xq_y^{\mathsf T})\,a_y^{-1}.
\]
The $9\times 9$ matrix $[Z_{yx}]_{y,x}$ is the product of the block column $[B_y]_y$ and the block row $[C_x]_x$, so its rank is at most $3$.

(i) Each $Z_{xx}$ is singular. Otherwise, for $y\ne x$, the $6\times 6$ submatrix on the blocks $x,y$ has rank $3+\operatorname{rank}(Z_{yy}-Z_{yx}Z_{xx}^{-1}Z_{xy})\ge 3+(2-1)$, because $Z_{yy}$ has rank at least $2$ and the correction has rank at most $1$. This contradicts the bound $3$. Hence $\det(I+p_xq_x^{\mathsf T})=1+q_x^{\mathsf T}p_x=0$, so $q_x^{\mathsf T}p_x=1$, $\operatorname{rank} Z_{xx}=2$ and $\mathrm{im}\,Z_{xx}=q_x^{\perp}$.

(ii) $\operatorname{rank} B_x=\operatorname{rank} C_x=2$. Both ranks are at least $\operatorname{rank} Z_{xx}=2$. If $C_x$ were invertible, then $Z_{yx}=B_yC_x$ would have rank at least $2$ for $y\ne x$, but $Z_{yx}=p_xq_y^{\mathsf T}a_y^{-1}$ has rank at most $1$. The same argument applies to $B_y$.

(iii) $q_y^{\mathsf T}p_x=\delta_{xy}$. By (i) and (ii), $\mathrm{im}\,B_y=\mathrm{im}\,Z_{yy}=q_y^{\perp}$. For $x\ne y$ the matrix $Z_{yx}=p_xq_y^{\mathsf T}a_y^{-1}$ is nonzero and its image $\mathbb{F}_2 p_x$ lies in $\mathrm{im}\,B_y$, so $q_y^{\mathsf T}p_x=0$.

(iv) Let $V$ be the row space of $[C_x]_x$, of dimension at most $3$. Each block row $B_y[C_x]_x$ has its rows in $V$. For $z\ne y$ the row $q_z^{\mathsf T}B_y[C_x]_x$ has $q_z^{\mathsf T}a_y^{-1}$ in block $y$, $q_y^{\mathsf T}a_y^{-1}$ in block $z$, and $0$ in the third block. Call it $v_{y,z}$.

(v) Fix a block $x_0$ and let $y,z$ be the other two indices. The projection of $V$ to block $x_0$ contains $q_z^{\mathsf T}a_{x_0}^{-1}$ for both $z\ne x_0$, and these are independent. Hence the vectors of $V$ that vanish on block $x_0$ form a space of dimension at most $1$. It contains the nonzero vectors $v_{y,z}$ and $v_{z,y}$, which are therefore equal. This gives $q_z^{\mathsf T}a_y^{-1}=q_z^{\mathsf T}a_z^{-1}$ and $q_y^{\mathsf T}a_y^{-1}=q_y^{\mathsf T}a_z^{-1}$.

(vi) Over the three choices of $x_0$ we get $q_x^{\mathsf T}a_t^{-1}=q_x^{\mathsf T}a_s^{-1}=q_x^{\mathsf T}a_w^{-1}$ for all $x$, where $t,s,w$ are the three indices. The $q_x$ form a basis by (iii), so the three first factors are equal, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:types}
No decomposition of length $22$ has type $(17,5,0)$, $(18,2,2)$, $(17,4,1)$, $(17,3,2)$ or $(18,1,3)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:types}
Every decomposition of length $22$ satisfies $\sum_t\operatorname{rank}(a_t)\ge 28$, and none has type $(19,0,3)$, $(18,2,2)$, $(17,4,1)$, $(17,3,2)$ or $(18,1,3)$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:l479}
In a decomposition of length $22$ with at least $14$ first factors of rank one, each line in the $G$-orbit of $L_0$ contains at most one first factor.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:lift}
The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item There are $a_t\in\bar a_t$ and two further terms with distinct first factors in $L$ that together with the terms $a_t\otimes b_t\otimes c_t$ form a decomposition of $T$ of length $22$.
\item At least two of the sets $V_{\chi_0}$, $V_{\chi_1}$ and $V_{\chi_0+\chi_1}$ contain a matrix of rank one.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix representatives $a_t^0\in\bar a_t$ and write $a_t=a_t^0+e_t$ with $e_t\in L$. As $e_t$ runs through $L$, the pair $(\chi_0(e_t),\chi_1(e_t))$ takes each value in $\mathbb{F}_2^2$ once. For a choice of the $e_t$ the tensor $T-\sum_ta_t\otimes b_t\otimes c_t$ maps to $0$ in $(A/L)\otimes B\otimes C$, so it equals $p\otimes M_p+q\otimes M_q$ for some matrices $M_p$ and $M_q$. Contracting with $\chi_0$, $\chi_1$ and $\chi_0+\chi_1$ shows that $M_p$, $M_q$ and $M_p+M_q$ are the elements of $V_{\chi_0}$, $V_{\chi_1}$ and $V_{\chi_0+\chi_1}$ given by this choice. Two terms with distinct first factors $x,y\in L$ and nonzero second and third factors have the form $x\otimes N_x+y\otimes N_y$ with $\operatorname{rank} N_x=\operatorname{rank} N_y=1$. Since
\[
p\otimes M_p+q\otimes M_q=p\otimes(M_p+M_q)+(p+q)\otimes M_q=q\otimes(M_p+M_q)+(p+q)\otimes M_p ,
\]
the two terms exist for this choice exactly when two of $M_p$, $M_q$ and $M_p+M_q$ have rank one. The element of $V_{\chi_0}$ depends only on the bits $\chi_0(e_t)$, that of $V_{\chi_1}$ only on the bits $\chi_1(e_t)$, and that of $V_{\chi_0+\chi_1}$ only on their sums. Any two of these three families of bits can be chosen independently. Hence two of the three matrices can be made of rank one by the same choice if and only if each of them can be made of rank one by some choice.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By symmetry it suffices to treat $L_0$. Suppose two first factors lie in $L_0$. They are distinct by Corollary~\ref{cor:distinct}, and the capacity of $L_0$ is $2$, so the third nonzero matrix of $L_0$ is not a first factor. The other $20$ terms project to a decomposition of $T_{L_0}$ of length $20$ with nonzero factors, and its coset profile $n$ satisfies \eqref{eq:coset} with $\ell-1=20$. At most one of the two first factors in $L_0$ has rank one, so at least $13$ of the other $20$ have rank one. Only $39$ of the $127$ nonzero cosets of $L_0$ contain a matrix of rank one, which gives the additional inequality
\[
\sum_{x\in C_1}n(x)\ge 13,
\]
where $C_1$ is the set of these $39$ cosets. We enumerate the coset profiles that satisfy these inequalities, as in Section~\ref{subsec:profiles}, and run the completion search with target $T_{L_0}$ on each. When it finds decompositions of $T_{L_0}$ with a given profile, we list all of them and check that for each at most one of the three sets in Lemma~\ref{lem:lift}(b) contains a matrix of rank one. By Lemma~\ref{lem:lift} no profile comes from a decomposition of $T$ of length $22$. The enumeration has $737{,}787{,}637{,}822$ nodes and $189{,}298{,}650{,}178$ leaves. For $10$ of the profiles the completion search finds decompositions of $T_{L_0}$, $540$ in all, and none of them lifts.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:adm}
A set $F\subset A\setminus\{0\}$ with $|F|=22$ is \emph{admissible} if
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $|F\cap S|\le\operatorname{cap}(S)$ for every subspace $S$ in the family $\mathcal{K}$ described below, and
\item $|\{a\in F: \varphi(a)=1\}|\ge 3\operatorname{rank}\varphi$ for every nonzero linear form $\varphi$ on $A$,
\end{enumerate}
and, in case (II), in addition
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),resume]
\item the type of $F$ is not excluded by Corollary~\ref{cor:types}, and
\item each line in the $G$-orbit of $L_0$ (Section~\ref{sec:l479}) contains at most one element of $F$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:canon}
Every $G$-orbit of sets contains a canonical set, and every initial segment of a canonical set is canonical.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The first claim is clear, since orbits are finite. For the second, let $F$ be canonical and $F_0=\{a\in F:a<c\}$. Suppose that $gF_0<F_0$ for some $g\in G$, and let $m$ be the smallest element of $gF_0\triangle F_0$. Then $m\in gF_0\setminus F_0$. If $m>c$, every element of $F_0$ is smaller than $m$ and therefore lies in $gF_0$, so $F_0=gF_0$ because both have the same size. This is impossible, so $m<c$. Every element of $F$ smaller than $m$ then lies in $F_0$, hence in $gF_0\subseteq gF$, while $m\in gF\setminus F$. Hence the smallest element of $gF\triangle F$ lies in $gF$, that is, $gF<F$. This contradicts the choice of $F$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:search}
Every canonical admissible set appears as a leaf of the search, and no leaf is the set of first factors of a decomposition of $T$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Suppose $T$ has a decomposition of length $22$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:distinct} its first factors form a set $F$ of size $22$, admissible by the remark after Definition~\ref{def:adm}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:canon} some $gF$ with $g\in G$ is canonical, and $gF$ is the set of first factors of a decomposition because $g$ extends to a symmetry of $T$. This contradicts Proposition~\ref{prop:search}. Hence $R_{\mathbb{F}_2}(\langle 3,3,3\rangle)\ge 23$, and Laderman's algorithm gives equality.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:W}
Let $W=\{a\in A: u^{\mathsf T}a=0\}$ or $W=\{a\in A: av=0\}$ with $u,v\in\mathbb{F}_2^3$ nonzero. In a decomposition of length at most $22$, at most $11$ first factors lie in $W$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The transposition symmetry of Section~\ref{sec:prelim} exchanges the two kinds of subspaces, and the symmetries \eqref{eq:sym} act transitively on each kind. So we may assume that $W=W_0$ is the space of matrices with zero third row. Let $O$ be the set of terms with $a_t\notin W_0$ and $I$ the set of the others. Let $\pi\colon A\to A/W_0$ be the projection, which records the third row. Then
\[
\sum_{t\in O}\pi(a_t)\otimes b_t\otimes c_t=(\pi\otimes 1\otimes 1)(T)=\sum_{j,k}\pi(e_{3j})\otimes e_{jk}\otimes e_{k3}.
\]
Read as a linear map from $B^*$ to $(A/W_0)\otimes C$, the right side is injective with image $(A/W_0)\otimes C'$, where $C'$ is spanned by $e_{13},e_{23},e_{33}$. The left side factors through the map $N\colon B^*\to\mathbb{F}_2^{O}$, $\beta\mapsto(\beta(b_t))_t$, so $N$ is injective, $|O|\ge 9$, and the map $e_t\mapsto\pi(a_t)\otimes c_t$ sends the image of $N$, of dimension $9$, onto $(A/W_0)\otimes C'$. With $\rho\colon C\to C/C'$, the tensors $\pi(a_t)\otimes\rho(c_t)$ for $t\in O$ therefore span a space of dimension at most $s=|O|-9$. Each of them has rank at most one, and $\pi(a_t)\ne 0$, so all $\rho(c_t)$ lie in the span of at most $s$ of the vectors $\rho(c_t)$. Hence the third factors $c_t$ with $t\in O$ lie in a subspace $D\supseteq C'$ of $C$ of dimension at most $3+s$. Projecting the third factor to $C/D$ removes the terms of $O$, so the rank of $T$ modulo $D$ in the third factor is at most $|I|$. Since $T$ is invariant under the cyclic permutation of its three factors, this rank equals $R(D')$, where $D'\subseteq A$ has the same matrices as $D$. If $s\le 1$, then $D'$ is a subspace of dimension at most $4$ containing the space of matrices supported on the third column, and by \cite{RR26} each such subspace has $R(D')\ge 14$. This contradicts $R(D')\le|I|\le 22-|O|=13-s$. So $s\ge 2$ and $|I|\le 11$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:planes}
In a decomposition of length $22$ with at least $14$ first factors of rank one, each plane in the $G$-orbit of $E_{436}$ or of $E_{422}$ contains at most two first factors.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:liftplane}
Let $E$ be a plane and $T_E=\sum_{t=1}^{19}\bar a_t\otimes b_t\otimes c_t$ a decomposition with nonzero factors. For a linear form $\varphi$ on $A$ let $W_\varphi=T(\varphi)+\operatorname{span}\{b_tc_t^{\mathsf T}:1\le t\le 19\}$. Suppose that for each set $P$ of three nonzero elements of $E$ there is a form $\varphi$ such that every matrix in $W_\varphi$ has rank greater than the number of $x\in P$ with $\varphi(x)=1$. Then there are no $a_t\in\bar a_t$ and three terms with distinct first factors in $E$ that complete the $19$ terms to a decomposition of $T$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose such terms exist, with first factors in a set $P$. Contracting the decomposition of $T$ with $\varphi$ gives $T(\varphi)+\sum_t\varphi(a_t)b_tc_t^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{x\in P,\,\varphi(x)=1}u_xv_x^{\mathsf T}$ for some vectors $u_x,v_x$. The left side lies in $W_\varphi$, and the right side has rank at most the number of $x\in P$ with $\varphi(x)=1$, contrary to the choice of $\varphi$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:eqf}
Each decomposition of $T_E$ becomes canonical after exchanges within the groups, and the exchanges do not change whether it lifts.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $\Phi=\sum_t t\,(512\,b_t+c_t)$. Exchanging an inverted pair $u<v$ in a group raises $\Phi$ by a positive amount, and $\Phi$ is bounded, so repeated exchanges end at a canonical decomposition. Both properties are invariant under exchanges because they depend only on the multiset of terms.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We follow the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:l479}. Suppose that three first factors lie in $E=E_{436}$ or $E=E_{422}$. They are distinct by Corollary~\ref{cor:distinct}, and at most one of them has rank one, so at least $13$ of the other $19$ have rank one. The other terms project to a decomposition of $T_E$ of length $19$, whose coset profile on the $63$ nonzero cosets of $E$ satisfies \eqref{eq:coset} and $\sum_{x\notin C_1}n(x)\le 6$, where $C_1$ is the set of cosets that contain a matrix of rank one. We enumerate these profiles up to the stabilizer of $E$. Table~\ref{tab:planes} gives the size of the two enumerations. Inside the enumeration, the completion search with target $T_E$ refutes every leaf except the external ones, whose certificates are too long, whose search exceeds a budget, or which admit decompositions of $T_E$. A separate run of the completion search refutes most external leaves. For the others, decompositions of $T_E$ exist, and Lemma~\ref{lem:liftplane} shows that none of them lifts, with Lemma~\ref{lem:eqf} reducing the decompositions to be tested.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
